messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 45-year-old agricultural worker who lives with his partner in a rural farming community. He came to therapy at his partner’s urging, though he is unsure what talking can do. The traumatic event that reshaped his life happened when he was eight years old, in a small house in Ghana. He watched his father beat his mother for what felt like hours—her cries, the thud of fists, the sound of her body hitting the floor. Kwame stood frozen in the doorway, too small to intervene, too terrified to run. He has never forgotten the helplessness that locked his legs that night, and he has never forgiven himself for doing nothing.

In the years since, Kwame has carried a quiet but absolute certainty that he is no longer the person he used to be. He used to be a happy man, quick to laugh, easy in company. Now he is always miserable, and he has lost his faith in people, in life, in anything higher. He will never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, even though he was only a child. That guilt has calcified into a belief that he is fundamentally broken, that happiness was something he squandered long ago. Because he sees himself this way—as someone who failed when it mattered most—he has come to feel that danger is everywhere. If he could not trust his own home as a boy, how can he trust any place or person now? Even when others tell him he is safe, he finds it impossible to believe them. This relentless sense of threat has made him hypervigilant; he is constantly scanning, watching, waiting for the next blow to fall, even though no one has raised a hand to him in decades.

The hypervigilance is worst at night. Kwame finds it harder to feel safe after dark than during the day, when he can at least see what is coming. To manage this fear, he has developed a strict set of rules. He makes sure he is never alone with another person—not in a truck, not in a field, not in a room. If his partner leaves the house, he steps outside and stands where neighbors can see him. He avoids closed doors. He has also begun to ruminate obsessively about getting even with his father, replaying fantasies of confrontation, of revenge, of finally making him pay. These thoughts give him a strange, bitter focus, but they also keep the past alive. At the same time, he tries hard not to think about the trauma at all, pushing memories away during the day, only to find they surface in fragments during sleepless nights.

These strategies have not brought him peace. Instead, they have deepened his misery and his guilt. Never being alone means he is always performing calm, always hiding the vigilance that exhausts him. The rumination feeds his anger and his sense of injustice, and the thought suppression leaves him feeling brittle, as though the trauma is pressing against a thin wall inside him. Each time he catches himself scanning a room or flinching at a shadow, he is reminded again that he is not the man he used to be. The strategies he uses to manage threat end up reinforcing his negative appraisals: he is broken, he is guilty, he has lost himself. And those appraisals, in turn, make the world feel even more dangerous. It is a loop that has tightened over decades.

At work, this cycle has concrete consequences. Kwame is a reliable laborer, but his coworkers have noticed he will not share a vehicle or work alone in a distant plot. He has turned down overtime that would require him to stay past sundown. His supervisor has expressed frustration, and Kwame has started to worry he will lose his job. His partner has grown tired of his refusal to be alone with her, interpreting it as rejection. Kwame knows this, but he cannot explain it. What finally brought him to therapy was a moment last week when his partner said, “I don’t know who you are anymore.” That sentence echoed his own inner voice. He is afraid he will never feel safe again, and he is equally afraid that the person he used to be is gone for good. But he is here, sitting in the chair, because some small part of him still hopes that might not be true.
